## 2 Kings 9 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: *"Now Elisha the prophet summoned one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, 'Tuck your cloak under your belt, take this flask of oil, and go to Ramoth-gilead.'"*

- **Elisha sends a young prophet rather than going himself.** Ellicott notes the Hebrew construction indicates "meanwhile Elisha had called"—i.e., while Joram was lying ill of his wounds. The timing was contemporaneous with Joram's recovery in Jezreel. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"Sons of the prophets"** refers to a prophetic training community—like a spiritual seminary. Precept Austin emphasises these were not biological sons but disciples in a prophetic guild; they were part of the believing remnant God preserves in every generation. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary]
- **Jewish tradition** (Seder Olam, followed by Rashi and Gill) identifies this unnamed prophet as Jonah son of Amittai (2 Kings 14:25). David Guzik notes this is "scarcely to be called a tradition," more a rabbinic fancy. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/] and [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]
- **"Gird up your loins"** means gathering up long robes and tucking them into the belt, an idiom for urgent preparation. Precept Austin: "It conveys alertness, discipline, and intentional readiness, moving from rest to resolve." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary]
- **The flask of oil** (Hebrew *pak*) was the instrument of divine appointment. Pulpit Commentary notes oil was commonly kept in open-mouthed jars of stone, glass, or alabaster. This was ordinary oil, not necessarily the holy anointing oil of the sanctuary. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/9-1.htm]
- **Ramoth-gilead** was a strategic border city east of the Jordan, contested between Israel and Aram. Precept Austin notes God chooses this volatile military setting to act, showing His purposes move forward amid political tension. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary]

### v. 2: *"When you arrive, look for Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi. Go in, get him away from his companions, and take him to an inner room."*

- **Jehu's name** means "Yahweh is He." Bob Utley (cited on Precept Austin) notes the Hebrew spelling of Jehu is similar to that of YHWH, both deriving from "to be." He was a military commander, not of royal lineage. This begins a new dynasty. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary]
- **Jehu is "son of Nimshi"**: Gill notes Jehu is commonly referred to as son of Nimshi (his grandfather) rather than Jehoshaphat. The Church Pulpit Commentary speculates there were fathers then, as now, "whom the children would willingly forget." He was probably left in supreme command at Joram's departure (Josephus). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"An inner room"** — literally "a chamber within a chamber." Ellicott notes this phrase is rare (occurring also in 1 Kings 20:30 and 22:25), which Thenius sees as a mark of common authorship. Secrecy was essential: the anointing of a rival king during wartime was treasonous and politically explosive. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html] and [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]
- MacArthur (cited on Precept Austin): "The rite was to be a secret affair without Elisha present so that Jehoram would not suspect that a coup was coming." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary]

### v. 3: *"Then take the flask of oil, pour it on his head, and declare, 'This is what the LORD says: I anoint you king over Israel.' Then open the door and run. Do not delay!"*

- **The abbreviated message**: JFB notes that only the chief part of the message is recorded here; the full announcement is found in vv. 7–10. The writer of Kings avoids needless repetition. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_kings/9.htm]
- **"Flee and do not delay"** — Ellicott explains this was "so as to avoid all questioning, and to give greater force to the act." The young prophet was not to linger or be interrogated. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Jehu is the only king of the Northern Kingdom to be formally anointed.** Constable (citing Wiseman): this indicates he was meant to follow the Davidic tradition. David Guzik adds: "Saul and David were anointed as king over Israel before they actually possessed the throne" — so Jehu's actual possession would follow later. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

### v. 4: *"So the young prophet went to Ramoth-gilead."*

- **The young man's identity**: Ellicott notes the unusual Hebrew construction ("the young man of the prophet"), with some MSS, the LXX, and Syriac omitting the second "young man," yielding "So the young man, the prophet, went." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Gill** remarks that the repetition highlights the young man's suitability: he was young (fit for travel), less known (for secrecy), and a prophet himself (fit for the sacred act). Though the Targum calls him "a young man, a disciple of the prophets." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]
- **Pulpit**: "It argued great faith in this young prophet that he undertook so readily the execution of this command. For there was no small danger in anointing a new king." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/9-4.htm] (Matthew Henry's Concise)

### vv. 5–6: *"When he arrived, the army commanders were sitting there… Jehu got up and went into the house, where the young prophet poured the oil on his head…"*

- **Jehu's question "For which of us?"** — Gill suggests he may not have understood at first, or he wanted the designation made plain to all the captains. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]
- **The anointing**: Precept Austin emphasises that pouring oil was "the ancient, God-ordained sign of divine appointment," signifying authority from the LORD Himself, not from popular support or military power. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary]
- **"Over the people of the LORD, even over Israel"** — the longer form in v. 6 underscores Jehu's covenantal accountability. Precept Austin: "Jehu is being appointed to rule God's people on God's behalf, under God's authority, and for God's purposes." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary]
- **The commission to Elijah** (1 Kings 19:16) was thus fulfilled by his successor Elisha, through this unnamed servant. David Guzik: "God's word may wait, but it never fails." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

### v. 7: *"You are to strike down the house of your master Ahab, so that I may avenge the blood of My servants the prophets and the blood of all the servants of the LORD shed by the hand of Jezebel."*

- **God as avenger**: Constable notes this is the only place in Kings where the writer emphasises Yahweh as avenging (cf. Nahum 1:2–3). Jehu was His instrument. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-9.html] (from search excerpt)
- **Jezebel's specific guilt**: Ellicott observes that the blood of "all the servants of the LORD" (beyond just prophets) is not recorded elsewhere, but "the thing is in itself probable, that Jezebel persecuted to the death those who clung to the exclusive worship of Jehovah." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Gill**: Jezebel "killed the prophets of the Lord, and caused to be put to death Naboth the servant of the Lord." The vengeance was to fall on her, her son Joram, and all her family. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]

### v. 8: *"The whole house of Ahab will perish, and I will cut off from Ahab every male, both slave and free, in Israel."*

- **"Him that pisseth against the wall"** — David Guzik notes the KJV's "graphic and explicit language" is the literal translation of the Hebrew for "male." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **"Shut up and left"**: Ellicott explains this refers to "him that is shut up and left" — the alliteration in Hebrew (*'atsur ve'azuv*) means every male without exception, whether imprisoned or at large, protected or abandoned. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]

### v. 9: *"I will make the house of Ahab like the houses of Jeroboam son of Nebat and Baasha son of Ahijah."*

- **Precedent dynasties**: Both Jeroboam's and Baasha's houses had been completely exterminated (1 Kings 14:10; 16:3–4). The fate of Ahab's house would mirror theirs exactly — total dynastic extinction. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary]

### v. 10: *"And on the plot of ground at Jezreel the dogs will devour Jezebel, and there will be no one to bury her."*

- **Exact prophetic fulfillment**: This echoes Elijah's prophecy in 1 Kings 21:23. Ellicott notes the Hebrew literally reads "and Jezebel the dogs shall eat." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Gill**: "or nothing of her to bury, as Kimchi, all being eaten up but her skull, feet, and the palms of her hands." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]

### vv. 11–12: *"Why did this madman come to you?" … "That is a lie!" they said. "Tell us now!"*

- **"Madman" (Hebrew *meshuggah*)**: The captains' dismissive label reflects how the world regarded God's prophets. Trapp (cited by Guzik): "So God's prophets were ever counted and called by the mad world." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **Jehu's evasive reply**: Ellicott says Jehu's "You know the man and his babble" carries emphasis on "ye" — Jehu implies the man was sent by his fellow-generals, sounding them out. Or more probably, it was simply evasion: "Why ask me, when you yourselves must have divined the right answer?" [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"It is false" (or "trickery!")**: Ellicott says this Hebrew reply (*sheqer*) is better rendered "trickery!" — meaning "you are pretending!" or "mere evasion!" The captains sensed Jehu was hiding something significant. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]

### v. 13: *"Quickly, each man took his garment and put it under Jehu on the bare steps. Then they blew the ram's horn and proclaimed, 'Jehu is king!'"*

- **Spreading garments**: This act was one of recognition, loyalty, and promise of support (Wiseman, cited by Guzik), similar to the triumphal entry of Jesus (Luke 19:36; cf. also the Roman custom). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **"On the top of the stairs"** (*gèrem*): Ellicott devotes significant space to this phrase. The Hebrew *gèrem* normally means "bone" (Aramaic *garmâ* = "self"). He suggests rendering "on to the body of the stairs" — an outside stairway leading to the roof serving as an improvised throne. The Targum renders it "at the steps of the hours," i.e., a sundial. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Instant enthusiasm**: Ellicott: "The instantaneous action of the generals shows that there must have existed a strong feeling against Joram in the army and an enthusiasm for Jehu which only required a word from him to precipitate a revolution." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Gill**: The captains "might come the more easily into such an acknowledgment of him as such, though he was anointed by one whom they had just called a mad fellow; being not so well affected to Ahab's family, and having a great respect for Jehu." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]

### vv. 14–15: *"Thus Jehu… conspired against Joram. (Now Joram and all Israel had been defending Ramoth-gilead against Hazael king of Aram, but King Joram had returned to Jezreel…)"*

- **Parenthetical background**: Ellicott calls vv. 14–15 a parenthesis explaining why Jehu commanded that no one escape the city. It repeats material from 2 Kings 8:28–29 to remind the reader of Joram's vulnerable position. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Israel had retaken Ramoth**: Ellicott states this is clear from the mention of "chambers," "the door," and the order to "let no man escape out of the city." Josephus expressly asserts this. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"If you commanders wish to make me king"** — literally "if it be your soul." Jehu secures the captains' full commitment before moving. The command to let no fugitive escape shows Ramoth was in Israelite hands, not under siege. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]

### v. 16: *"Then Jehu got into his chariot and went to Jezreel, because Joram was laid up there and Ahaziah king of Judah had gone down to see him."*

- **Joram's vulnerability**: Joram lay recovering from wounds; Ahaziah's presence meant both kings would be caught together. Gill notes the distance from Ramoth-gilead to Jezreel was approximately 24 miles (per Bunting's calculations). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]

### vv. 17–20: *The watchman sees Jehu's troops; two messengers are sent but do not return; "he is driving like a madman!"*

- **"Is it peace?"** — Ellicott insists Joram's question is not yet apprehensive but simply asks "What is the news?" He expected news from the army at Ramoth. If Joram had suspected treachery, he would not have sent a single horseman. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"What do you know about peace?"** — Ellicott calls Jehu's reply "a rough evasion: 'What business is it of yours, on what ground I am come?'" Jehu wanted to prevent alarm from being raised in Jezreel. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"Fall in behind me"** — both messengers were compelled to join Jehu's company, showing Jehu's popular support among the troops. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **"He drives like a madman"** — the word rendered "furiously" (*shiggâ'ôn*) is related to that rendered "mad fellow" in v. 11. Jehu's personality was discernible in his chariot-driving. Interestingly, the Targum and Josephus interpret this in the opposite sense: "quietly" or "slowly," suggesting Jehu was luring Joram out. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html] and [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

### v. 21: *"Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each in his own chariot, and met Jehu on the property of Naboth the Jezreelite."*

- **Providential meeting place**: The encounter on Naboth's vineyard is laden with poetic justice. David Guzik: "This was the land that Ahab and Jezebel had so wickedly obtained by murdering the innocent owner… On this very land — which, as far as God was concerned, still belonged to Naboth — the dynasty of Omri would meet its judgment." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **Gill**: "a very inauspicious place to meet him in." The location near where Naboth was stoned and his blood shed made the judgment unmistakably linked to Ahab's sin. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]

### v. 22: *"How can there be peace… as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?"*

- **Jehu's theological rationale**: Jehu frames his coup not as political ambition but as religious reform. Ellicott: "He assumes the part of champion of the legitimate worship against Jezebel and her foreign innovations." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"Whoredoms"** (*zenunim*): spiritual harlotry, i.e., idolatry. **"Witchcrafts"** (*kesapim*): sorceries, the use of spells and charms common among Semitic idolaters. Constable notes this was a capital offense under Mosaic Law (Exodus 22:18; Deuteronomy 18:10–12). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-9.html] (from search excerpt)
- **Gill**: Joram was guilty "at least in part; he connived at all in her, and did not attempt to restrain her, and therefore had no claim to peace, protection, and safety." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]

### vv. 23–24: *"Joram turned around and fled… Then Jehu drew his bow and shot Joram between the shoulders. The arrow pierced his heart…"*

- **Joram's cry "Treachery, Ahaziah!"**: Ellicott renders literally "Guile, or fraud, Ahaziah!" — Joram shouted these two words as he turned his horses to flee. He had come out without armour, unsuspecting. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"Drew his bow with full strength"** — a technical archery term: "filled his hand with the bow" (Wiseman, cited by Guzik). The shot went between the shoulders and exited through the heart — Joram's back was turned as he fled. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **Trapp** (cited by Guzik): "Jehu was an excellent marksman; but it was God that guided his hand, strengthened his arm (Ezekiel 30:24), and ordered his arrow (Jeremiah 1:9)." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

### vv. 25–26: *Jehu to Bidkar: "Pick him up and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite… the LORD lifted up this burden against him…"*

- **Jehu's eyewitness memory**: Ellicott emphasises this is the exact version of an eyewitness — Jehu himself had been riding behind Ahab when Elijah pronounced the oracle. The detail about "the blood of his sons" is not in 1 Kings 21 but preserved here. "The crafty Jezebel would not be likely to spare persons whose wrongs might one day prove dangerous." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Bidkar**: Ellicott notes the Syriac gives *Bar-dĕkar*, "son of stabbing" i.e., "stabber" or "slayer" — a very suitable name for Jehu's officer. The Hebrew name is probably a contraction of *Ben-dekar*. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"Yesterday"**: Ellicott explains that Ahab seized the vineyard the day after Naboth's murder — a detail not specified exactly in 1 Kings 21:16. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **"I will repay you on this plot of ground"**: David Guzik: "This confirms that Jehu saw himself as a fulfiller of God's will in bringing judgment on the house of Ahab." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **Trapp's vivid image**: "Jehoram's blood manureth that plat that was wrung from Naboth, and Jezebel shall add to this compost. Oh, garden of herbs dearly bought, royally dunged!" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

### vv. 27–29: *The death of Ahaziah king of Judah.*

- **Jehu kills Ahaziah without direct command**: David Guzik notes Jehu had no specific commission to kill the king of Judah, but "consciously or unconsciously, he was guided by God." Ahaziah was Ahab's grandson and had allied himself with Israel's wickedness. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **Ascent of Gur near Ibleam**: Ellicott notes these specific localities are marks of the account's greater trustworthiness. He fled to Megiddo and died there. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Reconciliation with 2 Chronicles 22**: The accounts differ in detail but are reconcilable. David Guzik notes Adam Clarke carefully works out the details. The Chronicles account says Ahaziah was found hiding in Samaria, brought to Jehu, and put to death. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **Honourable burial**: Despite his ignominious death, Ahaziah received burial in Jerusalem "not for his own sake, but only because his ancestor Jehoshaphat was a godly man" (2 Chronicles 22:9). Gill: Jehu permitted this "because he was the grandson of Jehoshaphat, a sincere worshipper of God." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]
- **v. 29**: A synchronising parenthesis. Ellicott notes 2 Kings 8:25 says "twelfth year" while here it's "eleventh" — such differences are not remarkable since synchronisms between the kingdoms were not based on exact records; different computations might make the same year the eleventh or twelfth. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]

### vv. 30–31: *Jezebel paints her eyes, adorns her head, and taunts: "Have you come in peace, O Zimri, murderer of your master?"*

- **Jezebel's adornment**: David Guzik (citing Patterson and Austel): "Doubtless Jezebel's adornment was intended to create a queenly appearance in the face of impending death and served as a royal burial preparation." Knapp adds: "Her innate vanity manifested itself up till the last." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **"O Zimri, murderer of your master?"**: Jezebel calls Jehu "Zimri" after the assassin who killed King Elah (1 Kings 16:8–12). Guzik: "It was her way of calling Jehu a despicable rebel." It was also an implied threat: Zimri's brief reign was ended by Omri (Ahab's father and Jezebel's father-in-law). She was saying, "The dynasty of Omri will defeat you just like it defeated Zimri." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

### vv. 32–33: *"Who is on my side? Who?" … "Throw her down!"*

- **The eunuchs' swift betrayal**: The eunuchs "probably worked for Jezebel, but they quickly responded to Jehu's request for support. They probably had long despised this wicked, pagan queen." (Guzik) [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **Blood spattered on the wall and on the horses**: Trapp: "Her brains, that devised mischief against the servants of God, are strewed upon the walls." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

### vv. 34–35: *Jehu eats and drinks, then orders burial; only skull, feet, and palms found.*

- **Jehu's untroubled attitude**: After trampling Jezebel, Jehu went in and "ate and drank" — completely untroubled by the gruesome end. He then orders burial "for she was the daughter of a king" (her father was Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **Only skull, feet, and palms remain**: The dogs had devoured the rest, making burial impossible. This was precisely what Elijah had prophesied. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]

### vv. 36–37: *"This is the word of the LORD, which He spoke through His servant Elijah the Tishbite…"*

- **Exact fulfillment**: David Guzik: "God's promise against Jezebel and the house of Ahab was exactly and righteously fulfilled (1 Kings 21:19, 21:23–25)." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]
- **"No one can say: This is Jezebel"**: Her body was so completely destroyed that there was nothing left to identify or memorialise. Ellicott and Gill both stress the total ignominy — in ancient Near Eastern culture, the desecration of a dead body and lack of burial was a fate worse than death itself. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
- **Hosea's later word against Jehu's house**: Guzik notes Hosea 1:4 — "I will avenge the bloodshed of Jezreel on the house of Jehu" — showing that though Jehu was God's instrument, his excessive violence and failure to depart from Jeroboam's sins brought judgment on his own dynasty. This is a major theological point: God uses imperfect instruments but holds them accountable. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

## Points of Difference Among Protestant Traditions

### Reformed / Reformed Baptist (Piper, desiringgod.org)

John Piper, in an "Ask Pastor John" episode on Jehu, focuses on **Jehu's defective zeal** as the chapter's enduring lesson. While Jehu carried out God's command externally (destroying Baal worship and Ahab's house), 2 Kings 10:29–31 reveals he "did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam" and "was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD… with all his heart." Piper's key pastoral insight: **"It is possible to have a kind of zeal for God that loves the external forms of Christianity but does not love God."** The test is whether one loves Christ Himself or merely loves the trappings of religious zeal — "Am I excited about this new Christian political movement, or am I excited about Christ?" This reflects the Reformed emphasis on heart-religion and the danger of external obedience without inward love for God. [https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/zeal-for-god-gone-wrong]

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word, David Guzik)

Guzik's commentary emphasises the **supernatural orchestration** of events — the Spirit's spontaneous prophecy through the young messenger (v. 7: "either Elisha told him to say this… or he came under the inspiration of the Spirit… and spoke this in spontaneous prophecy"), the "madman" label recalling how Spirit-filled prophets were perceived, and Jehu being "consciously or unconsciously guided by God" even beyond his direct commission (killing Ahaziah). The emphasis is on God's direct, active, moment-by-moment guidance through His servants. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

### Baptist (Gill)

Gill's exposition (18th-century Baptist) is characteristically **detailed, scholarly, and focused on precise linguistic and historical detail** — the exact nature of the "box of oil," the rabbinic traditions, the etymology of names, the geographical distances, and the harmonisation of this account with 2 Chronicles 22. Gill's notes reflect a high view of Scripture's detailed accuracy and the value of Jewish interpretive tradition alongside Christian exegesis. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/9.htm]

### Anglican (Ellicott)

Ellicott's Commentary (1878) is notable for its **text-critical and philological precision**. He regularly notes manuscript variants (LXX, Syriac, Vulgate), Hebrew constructions, and historical-archaeological details (e.g., Shalmaneser's Black Obelisk, Assyrian magical tablets, the etymology of "Jezebel" as *immaculata* = "virgo," possibly the origin of "Isabel/Isabella"). His approach reflects the 19th-century Anglican scholarly tradition of integrating linguistic, archaeological, and historical study. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (netbible.org / bibleodyssey.org)

I was unable to access these specific sites within the search limits. However, Constable's Expository Notes (Evangelical, but engaging with modern scholarship) notes that Jehu is mentioned in the **Assyrian Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III** (841 BC), providing an objective date for this period in Hebrew chronology. The obelisk depicts Jehu (or his envoy) kneeling and paying tribute — the earliest known pictorial representation of an Israelite king. [Referenced at https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-9/]

Ellicott also recounts the Assyrian inscription: "The tribute of Jehu, son of Omri: I received from him silver, gold, a golden bowl…" — ironically calling Jehu "son of Omri" though Jehu had just exterminated Omri's dynasty. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-9.html]
